one_liner: Single-header C++11 JSON-to-struct binder; about 2.6x faster roundtrip than nlohmann/json on a third-party M1 benchmark.
what_it_does: Parses JSON directly into C++ structs and serializes structs back to JSON, with no DOM in between. You annotate a type with JS_OBJ(...) inside the struct or JS_OBJ_EXT(Type, ...) outside it, then call JS::ParseContext(json).parseTo(obj) and JS::serializeStruct(obj); errors come back as a JS::Error code plus makeErrorString(), never as exceptions. It also exposes a token-level JS::Tokenizer that can take input in chunks, a JS::Map for inspecting a field before choosing the target type, and relaxed parsing for config files (comments, unquoted keys and values, newline delimiters, trailing commas). It is not a drop-in replacement for nlohmann's dynamic json value API.
how_it_is_fast: There is no intermediate tree. A pull tokenizer yields key/value tokens that point into the input buffer, and a compile-time member table generated by the JS_OBJ macros dispatches each key to its member through an unrolled length-plus-memcmp comparison. Values are decoded in place: integers and doubles use a bundled copy of the author's float_tools (Clinger fast path for short significands and exponents, otherwise iterative 128-bit scaling; a Ryu-derived shortest-digit printer for output). Serialization writes into chunked buffers. Since commits of 30 September to 6 October 2025 (after the measured run; the measured header has no SIMD intrinsics), SSE2/SSE4.2/AVX2/NEON scans locate string ends, number ends and whitespace, with a scalar fallback.
when_to_use: You already map JSON to plain C++ structs with nlohmann's to_json/from_json and want 2-4x faster struct reads and writes without moving to a C++20/23 reflection library.
The toolchain is stuck at C++11/14 (old GCC, VS2015-era MSVC, embedded SDKs), which rules out Glaze (requires C++23) and reflect-cpp (C++20).
Human-edited config files where comments, unquoted keys and trailing commas should parse into typed structs.
Inputs that arrive in pieces or are very large, using the chunk-fed JS::Tokenizer instead of materializing a document.
A dependency-free single header with a permissive licence that you can vendor.
when_not_to_use: Top throughput is the goal: on the same harness Glaze (1.01 s roundtrip), yyjson (1.22 s), reflect-cpp (3.15 s), daw_json_link (3.29 s) and RapidJSON (3.76 s) all beat json_struct's 5.87 s, and Boost.JSON (5.38 s) is level with it or slightly faster.
You need a mutable dynamic JSON value with nlohmann-style operator[] editing; json_struct is built around fixed struct schemas (JS::Map is a read-and-dispatch helper, not a full document model).

Structs with many members: each incoming key is matched by a linear, compile-time-unrolled scan over member names (primary names first, then aliases), so cost per key grows with member count, unlike Glaze's hashed lookup.

Number-heavy data with large or very negative exponents: values outside the fast path are converted by multiplying or dividing a 128-bit integer by 10 once per exponent step, so 1e-300 costs hundreds of loop iterations, and the double path has no big-integer correctness fallback (only float gets one).
Strict schema validation by default: unknown keys are skipped and missing members accepted unless you change ParseContext's flags.

integration.dependencies: none (C++ standard library only; Catch2 is fetched only for the project's own tests and benchmarks)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (README: tested on GCC, Clang and Visual Studio 2015+); optional std::optional support turns on automatically at C++17, std::array needs JS_STL_ARRAY defined before the include, and std::chrono::time_point needs JS_STD_TIMEPOINT
integration.platforms: any; SIMD scanning paths for SSE2, SSE4.2, AVX2 and NEON are picked by compiler macros, with a scalar fallback and JS_DISABLE_SIMD to turn them off
integration.thread_safety: not documented; the header keeps no global mutable state that was seen, so use one ParseContext or Serializer per thread
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: replaces nlohmann's to_json/from_json struct binding with JS_OBJ macros and parseTo/serializeStruct calls, but has none of nlohmann's dynamic json value API, exceptions or JSON Pointer/Patch features

gotchas: Lenient by default: ParseContext::allow_missing_members and allow_unasigned_required_members both default to true, so unknown JSON keys are skipped and absent struct members leave old values in place, and parseTo still returns NoError. Set both to false for strict parsing. track_member_assignement_state (default true) also records each unknown key as a std::string; the benchmark harness turned it off in its roundtrip loop but not in its read loop.

Tokens and DataRef values point into the caller's input buffer, so the buffer must outlive the ParseContext; parsing into an existing object clears and refills vectors and strings and keeps their capacity.

Version measured versus version shipped: the June 2025 harness fetched master with GIT_SHALLOW. The master tip before 8 June 2025 was commit 6e69e4a (26 March 2025; the next commit is 10 June 2025), and that header (8,656 lines) contains no SSE/AVX/NEON code. The numbers therefore describe the pre-SIMD scalar parser. The SIMD tokenizer and 'More optimizations' landed 30 September to 6 October 2025, and more parse and serialize performance commits landed 4 July 2026 (the current header is 10,315 lines). Current builds are probably faster, but no published number backs that.

Correctness fixes after the measured run (commit f5bf752, July 2026): \u escapes for U+0800..U+FFFF were decoded with a wrong UTF-8 lead byte (0xd0 instead of 0xe0; the line is still present in 6e69e4a), surrogate pairs were not combined, malformed integers such as '12-3' were silently truncated, and NaN/Inf were written as bare nan/inf (invalid JSON). The benchmark input has no \u escapes, malformed integers or non-finite values, so the measured numbers are not affected, but older vendored copies of the header carry these bugs.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick json_struct over Glaze or reflect-cpp only when you cannot use C++23 (Glaze) or C++20 (reflect-cpp), or when you want relaxed config-file parsing into structs; on speed alone they are 1.9-5.8x faster on the same roundtrip harness. Against Boost.JSON (about the same speed) and RapidJSON (faster), json_struct binds straight to structs without hand-written DOM walking or SAX handlers.
verified_claims_summary: In stephenberry/json_performance (results dated 8 June 2025; MacBook Pro M1, single core, Clang 17, 1,000,000 iterations of one ~0.6 KB object), json_struct from master took 5.87 s for parse-plus-serialize roundtrips against 15.44 s for nlohmann/json v3.11.3 (about 2.6x), with 178 vs 86 MB/s write (2.1x) and 316 vs 81 MB/s read (3.9x) (derived from page data). nlohmann's time includes building its DOM (json::parse then get<obj_t>; j = obj then dump) and a fresh obj_t each read, while json_struct reads into a reused object. An earlier run of the same harness (9 August 2024, Clang 15, preserved in the Loki-Astari fork) gave 5.50 s vs 15.71 s, 182 vs 84 MB/s and 326 vs 80 MB/s, consistent with the 2025 run.
status_note: Actively maintained (630 commits, last commit 29 August 2026, ClusterFuzzLite fuzzing and ASan/MSan CI on PRs). The single header is easy to vendor under an HPND-style permissive licence with no patent grant. The project publishes no benchmark numbers of its own (performance/benchmark.cpp is a Catch2 suite with no results), and the only harness numbers predate its SIMD rewrite and the July 2026 correctness fixes.
